newsitem.title: GERMANY: German think-tanks say EMU deficit target in reach.
newsitem.headline: German think-tanks say EMU deficit target in reach.

text.p: Germany's six leading economic institutes gave Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government a boost on Tuesday by saying they believed Bonn could still meet the tough deficit target for Europe's planned single currency.

But with their forecasts suggesting that economic growth this year would fall below Bonn's official 2.5 percent estimate, they urged the government to act quickly to carry out fiscal reforms to consolidate state budgets.

German finance minister Theo Waigel welcomed the spring report of the six institutes and said the government would be doing all in its power to meet the Maastricht criterion for monetary union limiting public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"The government will do everything necessary to achieve this goal...But possible requirements for actions can only be determined after presentation of the May tax estimates," he said, referring to next month's critical tax assessment report.

The six institutes forecast Germany's budget deficit at between 3.0 and 3.2 percent of GDP for this year, the timeframe that will determine EMU entry in 1999. The lower end of their forecast is the "point-landing" on the criterion that Germany has pledged to achieve.

But the independent forecasters estimated that GDP growth this year would grow by just 2.25 percent and only rise to 2.75 percent the year after, suggesting a slower rate of economic recovery than the government is hoping for.
Moreover, they forecast average unemployment of 4.28 million over this year, slightly higher than the 4.2 million average on which Bonn is basing its fiscal calculations.

They said it was now above all important that Bonn acts to remove damaging uncertainty about whether it would meet the Maastricht criteria by laying out its financial policies for the rest of the year as soon as possible.

"Uncertainty about achieving the Maastricht criteria and doubts about the consistency of fiscal policies have in fact led to misunderstandings that have considerably burdened the economic climate," they said in their report.

On the positive side, the institutes said no interest rate rise was in sight from the Bundesbank this year unless there was a need to protect the mark from a sharp movement upwards in the dollar. They forecast a small rate increase early next year.
The dollar moved slightly ahead to just under 1.71 marks as the institutes said they saw the U.S. currency at an average 1.80 marks in 1998.
Longer-term, the spring report also contained some good news for the employment situation in Germany, where joblessness is stuck at record highs.

It said that wage agreements and moves to reduce labour costs over the last year was leading to an increase in Germany's international competitiveness, forecasting a 1.5 percent drop in west German labour costs over 1996-1997.
Labour costs in the United States and the rest of Europe would meanwhile rise six percent and three percent respectively, they forecast.
